title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 10
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A bakery reduced the quantity it bakes each morning after finding that a fifth of its bread went unsold. In the following months, unsold bread fell to almost nothing, and the manager concluded that the reduction had eliminated waste without cost.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager's conclusion?
options: A. The bakery donates unsold bread to a shelter.
B. Flour prices rose during the period.
C. Customers arriving after four in the afternoon now regularly find the shelves empty, and several have moved to a competitor.
D. The bakery bakes several varieties of bread.
E. Some customers buy bread only at weekends.
questions.explanation: Lost sales are a cost that never appears as waste; the measure improved because demand went unserved. C affects margins but not the claim about waste.

questions.prompt: An airline reduced the space between rows in its cabins, fitting more seats on each aircraft, and reports that revenue per flight has risen. It concludes that reducing seat pitch is profitable.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Passengers do not notice the reduced space.
B. The aircraft can carry the additional weight.
C. Competing airlines will not reduce their seat pitch.
D. Fuel costs will remain stable.
E. The additional revenue is not outweighed by losses from passengers who choose other airlines because of the reduced space.
questions.explanation: Revenue per flight is measured now; profitability of the change requires that it not be eroded by passengers leaving. A is stronger than needed - passengers may notice and still fly.

questions.prompt: A ferry operator moved its morning sailing thirty minutes earlier and reports that the sailing now carries more passengers. It concludes that the earlier departure suits travellers better.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The ferry is not full even at the new time.
B. The operator cancelled a competing sailing run by another company at a similar hour, and its passengers transferred.
C. The crossing takes ninety minutes.
D. Ticket prices were unchanged.
E. Some passengers travel on foot rather than by car.
questions.explanation: Passengers absorbed from a discontinued rival explain the increase without any preference for the new time.

questions.prompt: A school introduced a uniform and reports that recorded behaviour incidents fell in the following year. The head teacher attributes the improvement to the uniform.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the attribution?
options: A. How much the uniform costs parents
B. Whether pupils like the uniform
C. How many pupils attend the school
D. Whether the school introduced other changes, such as a new behaviour policy or additional staff, in the same year
E. Whether neighbouring schools have uniforms
questions.explanation: Uniforms are rarely introduced alone; a simultaneous behaviour policy would explain the change. E offers a weak comparison without matched conditions.

questions.prompt: A blood service began offering donors a small payment and found that the number of donations fell. Officials had expected an increase.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains the outcome?
options: A. For many regular donors, giving blood had been an act of civic contribution, and payment reframed it as a poorly paid transaction they declined.
B. The payment was smaller than the cost of travelling to the donation centre.
C. Donation centres were open fewer hours than before.
D. The service advertised the payment only online.
E. Some donors are ineligible to give blood more than twice a year.
questions.explanation: The classic crowding-out result: introducing a price can displace a non-monetary motive that was doing more work than the price replaces. A explains indifference but not a fall below the previous level.

questions.prompt: Every bottle sold in the Ferndale scheme that carries a deposit is made of a single type of plastic. No container made of a single type of plastic is rejected by the recycling plant. Some containers collected in Ferndale are rejected by the plant.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. All deposit bottles are returned.
B. The recycling plant rejects containers only for reasons of material.
C. Some containers collected in Ferndale do not carry a deposit.
D. Most containers in Ferndale carry deposits.
E. Containers made of mixed plastics carry no deposit.
questions.explanation: Rejected containers exist; a deposit bottle is single-plastic and so is not rejected, therefore rejected containers carry no deposit. C and E overreach: E concerns all mixed containers everywhere, which the statements do not cover.

questions.prompt: A hospital reports that patients who receive an MRI scan within a day of admission have better outcomes than those scanned later, and proposes to scan all admitted patients within a day.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes scanners are available at all hours
B. ignores the financial cost of additional scans
C. does not specify which conditions were studied
D. overlooks that patients scanned quickly may be those whose condition made urgent scanning obviously appropriate
E. relies on outcome measures that are subjective
questions.explanation: Clinical triage sorts patients into the fast and slow groups, so the comparison confounds speed of scanning with the reason for it — and in either direction, since urgent cases may be sicker or more treatable.

questions.prompt: A company began paying part of employees' salaries in its own shares and reports that staff turnover has fallen. It concludes that share ownership makes employees more committed to the firm.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The share price has risen since the scheme began.
B. The shares cannot be sold until an employee has been with the company for three years, and departures rise sharply once that period has elapsed.
C. Some employees sell their shares immediately when permitted.
D. The scheme replaced a cash bonus of similar value.
E. Turnover has fallen across the industry.
questions.explanation: A vesting cliff produces retention through financial lock-in, not commitment, and the spike at three years is the signature of that mechanism. E is a rival explanation but a weaker one.

questions.prompt: An orchard owner observed that trees nearest her beehives produce more fruit than trees at the far end of the orchard, and plans to move all her hives to the orchard's centre so that every tree is close to a hive.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Hives are expensive to move.
B. The orchard contains several varieties of apple.
C. Bees are less active in cold weather.
D. Neighbouring farms also keep bees.
E. Bees forage over distances far greater than the length of the orchard, and the higher-yielding end also has deeper soil and better drainage.
questions.explanation: If foraging range already covers the orchard, proximity cannot be what produces the difference, and a plausible alternative cause is supplied.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer of kitchen appliances argues that the growth of the second-hand market for its products harms its business, since every used appliance sold is a new appliance not sold.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. assumes each second-hand purchase displaces a new one, when the resale value of a durable product may allow buyers to pay more for it when new
B. ignores the environmental benefits of reuse
C. overstates the size of the second-hand market
D. fails to distinguish between appliance types
E. does not consider the cost of servicing older appliances
questions.explanation: A liquid resale market raises what a buyer will pay at first purchase, so the effect on new sales is not the simple subtraction the argument assumes. A is true but does not address the business claim.

questions.prompt: A highways authority argues that spreading salt on roads before frost reduces accidents, citing that accident rates on treated roads are lower than on untreated ones. A critic replies that the authority treats the busiest roads first.
questions.question: The critic's reply weakens the argument by
options: A. denying that salt affects road surfaces
B. questioning the accuracy of accident records
C. suggesting that treated and untreated roads differ in ways that affect accident rates independently of treatment
D. arguing that salt damages vehicles
E. proposing that untreated roads be closed in frost
questions.explanation: Busy roads differ in design, lighting, speed and driver familiarity, so the comparison is not between like and like — though note the confound could run in either direction.

questions.passageTitle: Why Buyers and Sellers Tie Themselves Down
questions.passageText:
Where a market has many buyers and many sellers of an identical good, transactions can be settled on the spot and nobody needs a contract lasting years. A great deal of industrial trade is not like this, and the reason is usually a specific investment.

Suppose a supplier builds a plant next to a single customer's works because proximity is what makes the arrangement economic. Once built, the plant is worth far more in that use than in any other. The customer knows this and can demand a lower price, and the supplier, whose alternative is a stranded asset, may have to accept. The problem is not that either party is dishonest; it is that the investment creates a gap between what the asset is worth inside the relationship and outside it, and that gap is available to be captured.

The consequence is felt before anything is built. A supplier who anticipates the squeeze may decline to make the investment at all, or may build a less specialised, less efficient plant that keeps its options open. The loss is invisible, because it consists of arrangements that never happened.

Long-term contracts, joint ownership and vertical integration are all responses to this. Each has costs: contracts cannot specify every contingency, and integration puts activities inside a firm that the firm may manage poorly. Which response is chosen tends to track how specific the investment is and how hard the relevant contingencies are to write down — a prediction borne out across industries from coal and electricity to aluminium.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the hold-up problem arises because a specific investment
options: A. is more expensive than a general-purpose one
B. requires the supplier to borrow heavily
C. cannot be insured against physical damage
D. attracts competing suppliers to the same location
E. creates a gap between the asset's value inside and outside the relationship
questions.explanation: The passage locates the problem in that gap, and explicitly says it does not depend on either party behaving dishonestly.

questions.passageTitle: How Large Should a Reserve Be?
questions.passageText:
The number of species an area supports rises with its size, in a relationship regular enough to be expressed as an equation. In the 1970s this observation was applied to conservation, and produced a question that occupied ecologists for a decade: given a fixed area available for protection, is it better to create a single large reserve or several small ones?

The theoretical case for a single large reserve is that larger populations are less likely to be extinguished by chance, and that some species — wide-ranging predators above all — cannot persist in small fragments at all. The case for several small reserves is that they can capture more habitat types, spread the risk of a local catastrophe, and, if a region's species are unevenly distributed, together hold more species than one reserve of the same total area.

The debate ran long because it was posed as a general question that has no general answer. Which arrangement is better depends on how species are distributed in the particular region, on what threatens them, and on the ability of organisms to move between fragments — which itself depends on what lies between the reserves, a factor the original framing largely ignored.

The lasting contribution was not a rule but a reframing. Fragments are not islands in an empty sea; the intervening land can be hostile or permeable, and a network of small reserves connected by usable habitat behaves differently from the same reserves surrounded by hostile terrain. That insight redirected effort from the size question toward connectivity and the management of the land between protected areas.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the case for several small reserves rests partly on
options: A. the ability to capture more habitat types and spread the risk of local catastrophe
B. the lower cost of acquiring small parcels of land
C. the greater ease of protecting wide-ranging predators
D. the equation relating species number to area
E. the tendency of small populations to resist disease
questions.explanation: Those two reasons are given, along with uneven distribution of species. C describes an argument for a single large reserve.

B. ecologists disagreed about how to count species

questions.passageText:
Survey responses are commonly treated as measurements of pre-existing opinions. For a great many topics this is a poor description of what happens: respondents construct an answer at the moment of asking, using whatever the question and its context make salient.

The evidence is robust and, in places, uncomfortable. Offering a middle option changes the distribution of the remaining answers. Presenting the same policy as saving a proportion of lives or as losing the complement produces different support. The order of items alters the response to later ones, because an earlier question establishes a standard of comparison. Where a survey asks about an obscure matter, a noticeable share of respondents will express a view on something that does not exist, which is difficult to reconcile with the retrieval of a stored opinion.

None of this shows that surveys are worthless, and treating it as such is the commonest overreaction. Attitudes on subjects respondents have genuinely considered are more stable, effects of wording are often small relative to the differences a survey is used to detect, and a question repeated in identical form over time yields a trend that is informative even if its absolute level is not.

The disciplined conclusion is that a single figure from a single question deserves little weight, and that the useful products of survey research are comparisons: between groups asked the same question, or across time in the same words. What cannot be sustained is the interpretation of an isolated percentage as the public's settled view.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that respondents expressing views on matters that do not exist is difficult to reconcile with
options: A. the accuracy of sampling methods
B. the use of middle options in surveys
C. the stability of attitudes over time
D. the practice of repeating questions in identical words
E. the idea that answering consists of retrieving a stored opinion
questions.explanation: That finding is offered as evidence against the retrieval model of answering.

questions.passageText:
When a picture is cleaned, layers accumulated over centuries — varnish, dirt, earlier restorers' repaints — are removed. The operation is irreversible, and disputes about it have been among the fiercest in museum history.

The case for cleaning is that the varnish is not the artist's work. Natural resins yellow and darken, so a painting left untouched is not being preserved as painted but progressively altered, and removing that layer restores something closer to the original appearance.

The case against is not sentimentality about brown pictures. Varnish is difficult to separate from the paint beneath, particularly where the artist worked in thin glazes whose solubility resembles the varnish itself, and a cleaner may remove intended modelling along with discoloured resin. Historical restorers also repainted damaged areas, and it is not always clear where an old repair ends and original paint begins. The judgement is technical, but it is also aesthetic: how far back to go is a decision about which past state counts as the true one, and no measurement settles it.

Practice has shifted rather than resolved. Partial cleaning that thins rather than strips varnish, extensive documentation, testing on small areas, and reversible retouching that a later conservator can undo all reflect a change in what conservators think they are doing. The aim is no longer to recover an original that may not be recoverable, but to leave a work legible now and open to different judgements later — which concedes that the cleaner's own taste is one of the things being applied.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that leaving a painting uncleaned
options: A. preserves it exactly as the artist left it
B. is the practice recommended by most conservators
C. allows it to be progressively altered as the varnish yellows and darkens
D. prevents any future restoration
E. is possible only in controlled humidity
questions.explanation: This is the case for cleaning: an untouched painting is not preserved as painted but changing.

Presenting the same policy as saving a proportion of lives or as losing the complement produces different support. The order of items alters the response to later ones, because an earlier question establishes a standard of comparison. Where a survey asks about an obscure matter, a noticeable share of respondents will express a view on something that does not exist, which is difficult to reconcile with the retrieval of a stored opinion.

None of this shows that surveys are worthless, and treating it as such is the commonest overreaction. Attitudes on subjects respondents have genuinely considered are more stable, effects of wording are often small relative to the differences a survey is used to detect, and a question repeated in identical form over time yields a trend that is informative even if its absolute level is not.

The disciplined conclusion is that a single figure from a single question deserves little weight, and that the useful products of survey research are comparisons: between groups asked the same question, or across time in the same words. What cannot be sustained is the interpretation of an isolated percentage as the public's settled view.

readingPassages.title: Cleaning Old Paintings
readingPassages.text:
When a picture is cleaned, layers accumulated over centuries — varnish, dirt, earlier restorers' repaints — are removed. The operation is irreversible, and disputes about it have been among the fiercest in museum history.

The case for cleaning is that the varnish is not the artist's work. Natural resins yellow and darken, so a painting left untouched is not being preserved as painted but progressively altered, and removing that layer restores something closer to the original appearance.

The case against is not sentimentality about brown pictures. Varnish is difficult to separate from the paint beneath, particularly where the artist worked in thin glazes whose solubility resembles the varnish itself, and a cleaner may remove intended modelling along with discoloured resin. Historical restorers also repainted damaged areas, and it is not always clear where an old repair ends and original paint begins. The judgement is technical, but it is also aesthetic: how far back to go is a decision about which past state counts as the true one, and no measurement settles it.

Practice has shifted rather than resolved. Partial cleaning that thins rather than strips varnish, extensive documentation, testing on small areas, and reversible retouching that a later conservator can undo all reflect a change in what conservators think they are doing. The aim is no longer to recover an original that may not be recoverable, but to leave a work legible now and open to different judgements later — which concedes that the cleaner's own taste is one of the things being applied.
